## 11. Scripting (Luau 0.741)

### 11.1 VM ownership and sandbox

Native conversion of Luau tables into JSON or reflected values has a separate bounded allowance: `min(4 MiB, VM soft-limit bytes)`, charging 256 bytes per expanded value and entry and four bytes per string/key byte. Repeated aliases consume the allowance on every expansion, and traversal polls the inherited watchdog deadline. Exceeding this allowance rejects the input without advancing the VM allocator's breach count (ADR 0019 decision 10).
- **One `lua_State` per play session (and per loaded scene)**, created on Play and closed on Stop or `Scene.Load`, so no state leaks between sessions. Created with `lua_newstate(TrackingAllocator, …)`.
- **Memory limit (soft, with headroom).** `Scripting.MemoryLimitMB` (default 256) is a *soft* limit. The allocator keeps a reserved headroom of 16 MB above it and fails allocations only at the hard limit (soft + headroom), so the error handler, traceback capture and other instances can still allocate after a breach. Crossing the soft limit sets a flag; the next interrupt that is not a GC step (see the watchdog below) raises `script exceeded memory limit 256 MB in Board.OnFixedUpdate` in the current callback. The faulting instance is disabled and a full GC runs. Callbacks nested in the faulting call (another instance's `OnCreate` run by the same `Scene.Instantiate`) share that one memory fault instead of failing separately, so only the faulting instance is disabled; a new execution slice is refused until the recovery has run. An instance creation batch stops at the fault: the instances it has not made yet are created, and the `OnCreate` callbacks it has not run yet are run whole, at the next synchronization after the recovery: usually the next phase's start, before that phase's callbacks, but it can be a synchronization a binding triggers inside another callback (`Entity:SetActive`, `AddComponent("Script")`, `SetParent`), after that synchronization's enable and disable transitions, in canonical order either way, so no innocent instance is left half initialized by an `OnCreate` aborted at its first call. A timeout of the slice is handled the same way. A **second** breach in the same session, or reaching the hard limit at all, stops the session with a structured `memory` error (`play.state` reports it as `stopped` and `stopError`; `play.step` and `play.resume` then fail with `InvalidState` naming it, and a replay that stops this way fails with its `stopReason`). The VM is never left in an `LUA_ERRMEM`/`LUA_ERRERR` cascade, and the process is never out of memory.
- Libraries: `luaL_openlibs`, then `os` is reduced to nothing (no `os.time`, `os.clock`, `os.date`; `Time.GetRealTime()` is the explicit non-deterministic escape hatch), `math.random`/`math.randomseed` are rebound to the session stream, the transcendental `math` functions and `vector.angle` are rebound to DetMath (§4.12), `collectgarbage` and `gcinfo` are removed, and so are the escape hatches `io`, `package`, `debug`, `getfenv`, `setfenv`, `loadstring`, `loadfile` and `dofile` (environment reflection would expose another module's private globals), the engine API tables are registered, `require` is installed (a first-party C function that bounds the request, resolves it through `RequireResolver`, relative paths inside `Assets/` only, and records the edge, then runs the module through the engine's own module path: cached per VM, a cached nil apart from an absent entry, cycle-detected, and failing when the module's evaluation yields; nothing calls Luau's Require library, in any configuration, ADR 0030 decision 22), then `luaL_sandbox(L)` makes globals and libraries read-only, and `safeenv` is cleared afterwards so compiled fast calls dispatch through the rebound functions too (ADR 0019 decision 4). Each script module runs in its own thread (`lua_newthread` + `luaL_sandboxthread`) with private globals.
- **Watchdog.** `lua_callbacks(L)->interrupt` enforces a per-callback budget that counts the script thread's own CPU time (`Platform/ThreadClock.h`), not wall time, so no load from other threads or processes can time a callback out, while a runaway loop, which spends that CPU time, still times out (`Docs/Decisions/0039-script-budget-cpu-time.md`). Sampling a thread's CPU time costs a system call, so an interrupt compares `lua_clock()` with a wall deadline first, the budget after the callback began: the wall clock never runs slower than the thread's CPU time, so the budget cannot be spent before that deadline. Only once it has passed does the watchdog sample the CPU time the callback has used since it began, less excluded host work: with budget left the wall deadline moves to now plus what is left, otherwise the callback times out. On an unloaded machine CPU time equals wall time, so a player's hitch is still bounded by the budget; Windows accounts a thread's CPU time per clock tick (about 15.6 ms), so the budget holds to about one tick either way. The budget is `Scripting.CallbackBudgetMs` (default 1,000, minimum 10), applied in every configuration; Dist raises a smaller effective budget to 5,000 ms except in test runs, where per-suite overrides apply exactly (§6.1, §11.10). It is never disabled. **The interrupt returns immediately when `gc >= 0`**, without sampling either clock, because raising an error from a GC-step interrupt is unsafe; otherwise once the budget is spent it raises `script exceeded 1000 ms in Board.OnFixedUpdate (possible infinite loop)` (script file stem and callback; a module's top level reports `Board.<module top>`). Nested callbacks, such as `OnCreate` running inside `Scene.Instantiate` called from `OnFixedUpdate`, inherit the outer callback's deadline and budget instead of starting new ones, so nesting cannot extend the budget. Task and test-case resumes each get a fresh deadline. Host work that runs no Luau inside a callback does not count either: while `Test.Screenshot` renders and encodes its capture, or `Test.ReloadScript` reimports and type-checks the script, the wall deadline moves with the clock and the CPU time the work uses is credited (`ScriptEngine::RunHostOperation`), while the script's own Luau time, including Luau the host operation runs after all, still counts (ADR 0022 "Integration"). An agent-written `while true do end` cannot hang the editor or a shipped game.
- **Values from scripts are validated.** `Lua::Check<T>` rejects non-finite numbers, vectors, quaternions and colours with a located error naming the member (`<member>: argument #<n> contains NaN or infinity`, for example `Transform.Translation: argument #2 contains NaN or infinity`), and component writes enforce `FieldMeta` ranges (§5.4). Nothing a script computes can reach Jolt or the renderer as NaN, Inf, zero scale or a zero radius.
- **Host copies of script values are bounded** (`Scripting/ScriptLimits.h`), because one VM string can be copied into any number of host objects outside the VM allocator. A `Log.*` or `print` entry, and a `Test.Fail`, `Test.Skip` or `Test.Expect*` message, keeps at most 8 KiB: the host never assembles more than 8 KiB of the script's text, rewrites private chunk locations to authored ones, and then cuts longer text at a UTF-8 boundary and ends it with ` [truncated: <n> bytes]` (the full byte count of the script's text), the marker included in the 8 KiB (evaluation and load-time print capture too). One VM writes at most 1,024 log entries per (tick, frame) window and drops and counts the rest, with a warning when dropping starts and the count when the window ends; evaluation print capture keeps every line. `Debug.DrawText` text is at most 1 KiB, entity names at most 256 bytes, and an entity carries at most 256 tags of at most 256 bytes. A component field value a script writes (a proxy assignment such as `e.Text.Text = s`, or one `Entity:AddComponent` value) holds at most 4 KiB of text: its strings, map keys and Variant text together. `Test.Suite` and `Test.Case` names are at most 256 bytes and a `Test.ExpectScriptError` pattern at most 1 KiB. A suite registers at most 4,096 cases, `Test.Inject*` queues at most 1,024 events per input tick, a suite takes at most 256 `Test.Screenshot` captures (§11.10), `Audio.PlayOneShot` starts at most 1,024 one-shots per frame (§10.2), and a `require` request is at most 1 KiB, with at most 16,384 distinct require edges (importer, request, resolved path) recorded per VM. A retained value over its limit raises a located error before any mutation. Diagnostics retained for scripts are bounded as well. A script error keeps at most 8 KiB of message text (the value a script raises is captured that way, with the same cut and marker) and its 32 innermost traceback frames, the last of them then reading `[truncated: <n> more frames]`. Every script error stream (a VM's, a session's, the editor's or Runtime's history) keeps the 256 distinct errors with the latest occurrences, evicting the oldest; `script.errors` reports `evicted` to a reader whose cursor precedes an evicted error, and an evicted error that occurs again starts a new count. A running test case keeps at most 256 unclaimed script errors (a claim releases its error at once; a later one cannot be claimed and fails the case), and a report row keeps at most 32 failures for `Expect*` and unexpected script errors, the last then counting any further ones as `[truncated: <n> more failures]` (the row fails all the same), and a suite at most 1,024 such failures across its rows. Errors, log entries, captured output and test reports show authored `file:line` locations, never the VM's private chunk identities.
- **Identities are interned.** Entity, component proxy and `AssetRef` userdata are cached per VM while referenced, so one identity is one value: table keys and `rawequal` agree with `==`. A failed `require` forwards the child's structured error only within the execution slice that raised it; a copy a script keeps and raises later is a runtime error of the raising frame.
- **Bytecode trust.** Only bytecode compiled by the engine is loaded with `luau_load`; Luau does not verify bytecode, so pak entries are hash-verified before loading (§14.1).
- One OS thread uses the VM (the main thread).

### 11.2 Script shape and fields
```lua path=Assets/Scripts/Ball.luau
--!strict
export type Ball = ScriptInstance & {
	-- fields (declared below, resolved per instance)
	Torque: number, Goal: Entity?, GoalSound: AssetRef?, Checkpoints: { Entity },
	-- state
	Spawn: vector, Heading: number, ReachedGoal: boolean,
}

local Ball = {}   -- a plain table literal: unsealed in strict mode, so members can be added below

Ball.Fields = {
	Torque = Field.Number(30, { Min = 0, Max = 200, Tooltip = "Roll torque (N*m)" }),
	Goal = Field.Entity(),
	GoalSound = Field.Asset("AudioClip"),
	Checkpoints = Field.Array(Field.Entity()),
}

-- Above this horizontal speed (m/s) the heading turns towards the velocity, by at most this many degrees a tick.
local HeadingMinSpeed, HeadingStep = 2.5, 2

function Ball.OnStart(self: Ball)
	self.Spawn = self.Entity.Transform.WorldPosition
	self.Heading = self.Entity.Transform.EulerAngles.y   -- degrees, 0 facing -Z, positive turning left
	self.ReachedGoal = false
end

function Ball.OnFixedUpdate(self: Ball, dt: number)
	-- The control is relative to the ball's own heading, kept here in the fixed step; the follow camera reads it in
	-- OnLateUpdate. It never reads the camera's pose, which the camera writes in the frame phase: live play would then
	-- depend on the frame rate, while every lockstep run stays deterministic, so no suite would catch it.
	local body = self.Entity.RigidBody :: RigidBody
	local velocity = body:GetLinearVelocity()
	if vector.magnitude(vector.create(velocity.x, 0, velocity.z)) > HeadingMinSpeed then
		local toward = math.deg(math.atan2(-velocity.x, -velocity.z))
		self.Heading += math.clamp(Math.DeltaAngle(self.Heading, toward), -HeadingStep, HeadingStep)
	end
	local heading = math.rad(self.Heading)
	local forward = vector.create(-math.sin(heading), 0, -math.cos(heading))
	local right = vector.create(math.cos(heading), 0, -math.sin(heading))
	local move = right * Input.GetAxis("MoveX") + forward * Input.GetAxis("MoveZ")
	body:AddTorque(vector.cross(vector.create(0, 1, 0), move) * self.Torque)
	if self.Entity.Transform.WorldPosition.y < -20 then
		body:Teleport(self.Spawn)
		body:SetLinearVelocity(vector.zero)
	end
end

function Ball.OnTriggerEnter(self: Ball, other: Entity)
	if other == self.Goal and not self.ReachedGoal then
		self.ReachedGoal = true
		if self.GoalSound then
			Audio.PlayOneShot(self.GoalSound, self.Entity.Transform.WorldPosition)
		end
	end
end

return Script.Define("Ball", Ball)
```
- **The class pattern.** A behaviour builds its class as a local table literal and returns `Script.Define(name, class)`, declared `Define: <T>(name: string, class: T) -> T`. `Script.Define` registers the name and returns the same table, so the module's type is exactly the class literal's inferred type. This avoids adding members to a sealed table returned from a function, which the new solver rejects. The instance type is an exported alias (`ScriptInstance & {fields…, state…}`) used for `self`. The Behaviour, Module and Test templates follow this pattern. TypeChecker fixtures cover each template, a behaviour with every `Field` kind, and the cast idiom below, and CI type-checks every documentation example (§11.9).
- **Cross-script access.** `Entity:GetScript()` returns `any`, because the instance type depends on which script is attached. The idiom requires the other script's module for its type and casts: `local BallScript = require("./Ball")` then `local ball = other:GetScript() :: BallScript.Ball?`. Requiring a behaviour returns its class table, the same one the instances use. An entity holds several scripts as the slots of its Script list (ADR 0031 decisions 17 and 18): `GetScript()` returns the instance of its first slot, `GetScript(name)` the instance of the first slot, in slot order, whose behaviour's `Script.Define` name is `name` (`other:GetScript("Ball") :: BallScript.Ball?`), and `GetScripts()` the live instances of every slot, in slot order. Each returns nil, or leaves out, a slot without a live instance (no script, not created, or being torn down; a fault-disabled instance is still returned).
- Field kinds: `Number`, `Integer`, `Bool`, `String`, `Vector`, `Color`, `Quat`, `Entity`, `Asset(type)`, `Enum({...})`, `Array(kind)`. Field kinds map onto reflection `FieldType`s, and a script slot's `Fields` (`ScriptSlot.Fields`) is a `Map<Variant>` resolved against its slot's script's schema (§5.4), so the inspector, serialization and automation (`script.fields`) handle them generically.
- **Script kinds.** The importer classifies each script by what its module returns. A **Behaviour** returns the result of `Script.Define`. A **TestSuite** returns the result of `Test.Suite` (§11.10). Anything else is a **Module**: a plain library such as `Board.luau`, needing no `Script.Define`, loadable only through `require`. Only a Behaviour may be assigned to a script slot (`ScriptSlot.Script`); anything else raises `SCRIPT_NOT_A_BEHAVIOUR` (validation error, also returned by `entity.update`).
- **Load-time environment.** The `ScriptImporter` classifies the script and extracts the field schema by running the module's top level in a throwaway sandboxed VM. The VM is new for every import, but the API it binds is not rebuilt for each: the editor builds one frozen `PureScriptApi` when it starts (every built-in component type and binding, the registries a VM without one builds for itself, `Scripting/Sandbox.h`), and every import's VM borrows it, on any import thread, never touching its coverage counters (ADR 0041 decision 3). That VM contains every **pure** standard library (`math` with DetMath and a fixed-seed `random`, `string`, `table`, `bit32`, `utf8`, `buffer`, `vector`, `coroutine`), the pure engine modules `Script`, `Field`, `Color`, `Quat` and `Math`, the constructor `Test.Suite`, and a **load-time `require`**. Other engine APIs raise `<Module.Member>: is not available at load time` (for example `Input.GetAxis: is not available at load time`). The load-time `require` uses the same VFS resolver as the runtime one (relative to the script, inside `Assets/`, cycle-detected), runs each required module once in the same restricted environment, caches it for the duration of this import, and records the edge in `AssetDependencyGraph`. One 250 ms budget covers the whole require graph; it counts the import thread's own CPU time (`Platform/ThreadClock.h`), not wall time, so an import never fails because the machine was busy or the thread waited, and importers stay pure functions of their inputs (§7.4, ADR 0022 "Integration"). A module whose top level calls engine APIs fails import with a located message. Module tops must be free of engine side effects; building local tables (`table.freeze`, string formatting, kick tables) is fine. The `luau-gameplay` skill documents this.
- Overrides in a script slot's `Fields` with an unknown name or wrong type produce a validation diagnostic (`SCRIPT_UNKNOWN_FIELD_OVERRIDE`, `SCRIPT_FIELD_TYPE_MISMATCH`), fall back to the default at run time, and are preserved in the file until fixed.
- An instance is a table `{Entity = <Entity>, <resolved fields>}` whose metatable is the class table (`__index = class`). Every slot of an entity's Script list that names a script is its own instance, identified by (entity UUID, slot), with its own table, field overrides, `ExecutionOrder`, tasks, held physics events and fault state; the same script may fill two slots (ADR 0031 decision 17).

### 11.3 Lifecycle callbacks and order
**While the world is paused** (§5.6; M35, ADR 0050 decision 2) `OnFixedUpdate`, `OnUpdate` and `OnLateUpdate` reach only the instances whose behaviour class sets `RunsWhileWorldPaused = true` (a key of the class table beside `Fields`, a boolean, read by `Script.Define`, so a class sets it before the call; a hot reload defines the class again); every other callback (`OnCreate`, `OnStart`, `OnEnable`, `OnDisable`, `OnDestroy`, the `OnUi*` callbacks) reaches every instance as always. No new contact or animation event arises, since the world does not step, but the destroy flushes still close the pairs of the entities destroyed or switched off while the world is paused (their synthesized `OnCollisionExit` and `OnTriggerExit`), and the start flush still delivers the events held for an instance that starts then; both reach every instance, one that holds too, since gating them would leave an exit without its enter. A visual-scripting graph behaviour opts in through its document's `RunsWhileWorldPaused` (M39, ADR 0056 decision 6), which its transpiled class sets before `Script.Define`, so a pause menu may be a graph.

All optional: `OnCreate()`, `OnStart()`, `OnFixedUpdate(dt)`, `OnUpdate(dt)`, `OnLateUpdate(dt)`, `OnDestroy()`, `OnEnable()`, `OnDisable()`, `OnCollisionEnter(other, contact)`, `OnCollisionExit(other)`, `OnTriggerEnter(other)`, `OnTriggerExit(other)`, `OnHotReload()` (EditorOnly: hot reload exists only in the editor, §11.4), the 2D world's `OnCollisionEnter2D(other, contact)`, `OnCollisionExit2D(other)`, `OnTriggerEnter2D(other)`, `OnTriggerExit2D(other)` (M21, §9.9; the contact's vectors in the plane), M22's UI callbacks `OnUiClick(element)`, `OnUiValueChanged(element, value)` (a boolean for a toggle, a number for a slider), `OnUiFocus(element, focused)`, `OnUiHover(element, hovered)`, `OnUiCancel(element)` and `OnUiScroll(element, position)` (ADR 0033 decision 27), and C22.3's `OnUiTextChanged(element, text)` and `OnUiSubmit(element, text)` (a text input's Text as it is when the callback runs; ADR 0033 decision 47), each returning `boolean?`; `OnAnimationEvent(event)` (M23, ADR 0034 decision 31: `event` is `{Name, Layer, Clip, Time}`, Layer 1-based, Time in the clip; step 4c of §5.7, Play only); `OnLocaleChanged(locale, previous)` (M38, ADR 0055 decision 2: delivered synchronously by `Loc.SetLocale`, before it returns and under its caller's deadline, to every started, enabled behaviour that defines it, the caller's own included, in execution order from a snapshot taken before the first call, whether or not the world is paused; an instance created meanwhile hears nothing, its `OnStart` reading the new locale; a fault disables only its instance; `Loc.SetLocale` raises inside it and at teardown); and `OnJointBreak(force, torque)` (M37, ADR 0054 decision 8: the entity's joint broke at step 7's PostStep, after that step's collision and trigger callbacks, with the force in N and the torque in N m of the collision step that broke it; Play only; §9.10). Order and timing are defined in §5.7: callbacks run by (`ExecutionOrder`, canonical entity order), and with several scripts on one entity by (`ExecutionOrder`, canonical entity order, slot), the slot being part of the scene's data, so the order is identical in every run. Gameplay belongs in `OnFixedUpdate` (deterministic); `OnUpdate`/`OnLateUpdate` are for presentation (cameras, smoothing). `OnStart` is gameplay too: it runs once, before the instance's first update, in a start flush, either a scene's startup flush (at the session's start, after `Scene.Load` and `Scene.Reload`) or, for an entity created during the session, a fixed step's (§5.7 step 2), never the frame phase, so it reads the step view and the fixed delta whatever the frame rate (ADR 0038 decision 14). A scene transition gameplay code requests applies after its tick, one a scene's startup callbacks request after the next tick, and one `OnUpdate` or `OnLateUpdate` requests at that frame's end (§5.6, ADR 0038 decision 15). `Time.GetDeltaTime()` and input edges are phase-aware (§4.3).

**Several scripts on one entity** (ADR 0031 decisions 17 and 18). The callbacks addressed to an entity reach every slot's instance in slot order: a physics callback and an animation event reach each started slot, each slot holding or discarding its own held contacts and events; the `OnEnable` and `OnDisable` of an active-state change reach an entity's live instances together, in slot order, at the turn of its slot that comes first in (`ExecutionOrder`, canonical entity) order, while an entity switched on again before its disable was flushed keeps its instances, which get the `OnEnable` that pairs their `OnDisable` and keep their state, start state and tasks (M35, ADR 0050 decision 8; the outermost synchronization of the switch observes it, so a switch back on inside a destroy flush's own `OnDisable` callbacks still completes that flush's teardown), and instances recreated when an entity is enabled after its disable was flushed get `OnCreate` in (`ExecutionOrder`, canonical entity, slot) order and then `OnEnable` in canonical entity order and slot order; `OnDestroy` runs for one entity's slots in reverse slot order, children first. A fault disables only its own instance and cancels only its tasks, and the entity's other slots keep running; its error names the slot (§11.7). A write of the Script list (automation, the inspector or a script's component proxy) keeps an instance whose slot still holds the same script asset and destroys and creates the others, as removing and adding the component would. Hot reload patches the instance of every slot holding a reloaded behaviour. **Bubbling** is defined per behaviour; M22's six UI callbacks are the bubbling ones (ADR 0033 decision 27): a bubbling event visits its target entity, then each ancestor; at each entity every started, enabled behaviour that defines the callback receives it, in slot order; propagation to the next ancestor stops after an entity where any behaviour's callback returned true (the boolean; another value lets it go on), and that entity's other behaviours still receive it. The UiEvents phase (§5.7, after the start flush) delivers the events the UI raised (`ScriptEngine::DispatchUiEvents`): the walk is the target and the ancestors it had when the walk starts, so a callback that reparents an entity cannot lengthen or repeat it; an event whose target the scene no longer holds, or holds pending destruction, is dropped; an ancestor a callback of the event destroyed is passed over, the walk going on above it; a callback's fault disables only its instance, and the event goes on (§11.7). Non-bubbling callbacks ignore return values, so no slot can keep another from receiving one.

No callback reaches an instance before its `OnCreate`, and no `OnDestroy` follows without one, even when another script removes the instance while its creation batch is still running. Physics callbacks always run in the fixed step, the 2D ones like the 3D ones, and an instance holds both worlds' contacts in one queue, in arrival order. A contact that begins before an instance's `OnStart` (an instance created during steps 3–4, whose body appears at the same tick's `PreStep`) is held and delivered at the next fixed step's start flush, after `OnStart` and before `OnFixedUpdate`, in dispatch order, so every exit follows its enter (§9.4). Animation events follow the same rule: one that reaches an instance before its `OnStart` (created in steps 3–4 of the tick) is held, in the same queue as its held contacts in arrival order, and delivered at the next fixed step's start flush. Destruction or a fault discards held contacts and events.

Tasks: `Task.Wait(seconds)`, `Task.WaitTicks(n)`, `Task.Spawn(fn)`, `Task.Delay(seconds, fn) -> TaskHandle`, `Task.Cancel(handle)`, built on `lua_resume`/`lua_yield`, timed in simulation time (a wait of `seconds` lasts `ceil(seconds / FixedDelta)` ticks, at least one, where a quotient within a few ulps above an integer, such as 0.14 s at 50 Hz, counts as that integer), resumed at step 4 of §5.7, owned by the instance and cancelled when it is destroyed. A task counts the world's ticks when its owner is an instance whose class does not set `RunsWhileWorldPaused` (so its waits and delays hold while the world is paused, §5.6, and it is not resumed then), and the session's ticks otherwise (an opted-in instance's, a test case's, one without an instance owner; M35, ADR 0050 decision 2). Due tasks resume in the order of their due ticks, then their creation; a world-clock task's due tick and a session-clock task's are on different clocks, so once the world has held ticks a world behaviour's due task resumes before a menu's or a case's due in the same tick, whatever their creation order, which is deterministic, since both clocks are state. A task spawned by a lifecycle callback belongs to its instance even while a test case is running; only a case's own thread and the tasks it spawns belong to that case and end with it (§11.10). `Task.Spawn(fn)` creates a thread (`lua_newthread` + `luaL_sandboxthread`) and resumes it immediately until its first yield or its end. `Task.Delay` creates a thread that first runs when its time is due.

**Yield rule.** Luau raises "attempt to yield across metamethod/C-call boundary" when a coroutine yields with C calls on its stack beyond the resume point (`ldo.cpp`, `nCcalls > baseCcalls`). Callbacks are entered with `lua_pcall` from C++, so a callback body is not yieldable. The engine makes this explicit instead of letting it surface as an obscure VM message. `Task.Wait`, `Task.WaitTicks`, `Test.WaitTicks` and `Test.WaitUntil` check `lua_isyieldable(L)` first and, when it returns false, raise `Task.Wait can only be used inside Task.Spawn, Task.Delay or a Test.Case body` at the caller's line. Bodies of `Task.Spawn`, `Task.Delay` and `Test.Case` always run as resumed threads, where waiting works. A callback that wants a sequence writes `Task.Spawn(function() … Task.Wait(1) … end)`. Unit tests: "Tasks: Task.Wait in OnStart raises the documented error", "Tasks: Task.Wait inside Task.Spawn resumes at the expected tick", "Tasks: yielding inside a metamethod raises the VM error, caught as a script error". The `luau-gameplay` skill states the rule.

### 11.4 Binding layer
- Every API member is registered once, and each registration produces the binding, the `Engine.d.luau` declaration, the docs entry (mandatory description) and a **call counter** (active when test mode is on, in every configuration):
	- module functions: `api.Module("Physics").Function("Raycast", &ScriptBindings::Physics_Raycast, "(origin: vector, direction: vector, maxDistance: number, layerMask: number?) -> RaycastHit?", "Casts a ray and returns the closest hit or nil.")`;
	- userdata types: `api.Type("Entity")`, `api.Type("Quat")`, `api.Type("Color")` and one type per component proxy with methods (`RigidBody`, `CharacterController`, `AudioSource`, `Camera`, `MeshRenderer`, `Transform`, M23's `Animator` and `SkinnedMesh`, M26's `ParticleEmitter` and `Terrain`), each with `.Method(name, fn, signature, description)`, `.Property(name, getter, setter?, type, description)`, `.Operator("__mul" | "__eq" | "__add" | …, fn, signature, description)` and `.Constructor(name, fn, signature, description)` (e.g. `Quat.New`, `Color.FromHex`);
	- component proxy fields come from the type registry (§5.4) and are counted by gate 4;
	- **string-enum parameters** (e.g. `space: Space` of `Transform:Translate`) declare their enum, and each value gets its own counter when the enum has at most 16 values. An overloaded member can give one argument slot a different enum per overload, selected by another argument's Lua type: `Test.InjectGamepad(index, button: GamepadButton, state: InputEventState)` when the third argument is a string, `(index, axis: GamepadAxis, value: number)` when it is a number. Each overload's slot is validated before the callback and counted per value. Larger name tables such as `Key` are covered by table-driven unit tests.
- **Run modes.** Every callback, function, method and property has `RunModes`: `All` (default) or `EditorOnly`. The EditorOnly members are `OnHotReload` and `Test.ReloadScript`, plus any future member that needs the editor. Coverage gates are evaluated per run mode (§15.6). Members whose *behaviour* differs between modes, but which work everywhere (`Application.IsEditor`, `Debug.Break`, `Application.Quit`), are `All`, and their per-mode behaviour is documented and tested in each mode.
- `Bindings/Script.cpp` binds `Script.Define` and every `Field.*` constructor (also present in the load-time VM).
- Typed helpers `Lua::Check<T>(L, index)`/`Lua::Push<T>` give uniform errors: `Entity:AddComponent: argument #2 expected string, got number`; numeric checks also reject NaN and ±Inf (`<member>: argument #<n> contains NaN or infinity`).
- Userdata are tagged (`lua_newuserdatatagged`, one tag per type, metatables via `lua_setuserdatametatable`; payloads are trivially destructible identities, pushed with `lua_newuserdatataggedwithmetatable` and `static_assert`ed so, so no userdata destructors are registered); method dispatch uses `__namecall` with atoms (`useratom` callback).
- **No pointers cross into Luau.** `Entity` userdata holds `{UUID, SceneGeneration}` and re-resolves on every access; a component proxy holds `{UUID, ComponentTypeIndex}`. Proxies implement `__index`/`__newindex` from the registry (fields validated against `FieldMeta`; writes go through the reflected setter, which patches and notifies systems). A typed asset reference written by a proxy or passed to `Entity:AddComponent` must name an asset of its `TypedAssetHandle`'s type, at any depth of arrays, maps and structs: a handle the asset service registers with another type is refused with Validation naming the field and both types (M26, ADR 0037 decision 32; `ScriptProxy::ValidateAssetTypes`), while a handle it does not know is left to the readers and `project.validate`. Each proxy field read and write increments a `(component, field)` coverage counter in test mode. Transform has hand-written fast paths.
- Value types: 3D vectors are Luau's native **`vector`** (no allocation; library `vector.create/magnitude/normalize/cross/dot/angle/floor/ceil/abs/sign/clamp/max/min/lerp`; fields `.x .y .z`). 2D values (screen positions, `vec2` fields) are `vector` with z = 0. `Quat` and `Color` are tagged userdata with lowercase fields (`.x .y .z .w`, `.r .g .b .a`) to match `vector`. All other names are PascalCase.
- **Enums are strings**, typed in `Engine.d.luau` as singleton unions (`type BodyType = "Static" | "Kinematic" | "Dynamic"`), so the type checker catches typos. This covers `Key`, `MouseButton`, `GamepadButton`, `GamepadAxis`, `CursorMode`, `Space`, `AudioGroup` and every reflected enum.
- **Shortcut properties.** `entity.<ComponentName>` returns the component's proxy, or nil when the component is absent, for every component that is ScriptVisible and not `Hidden`, `EntityLevel` or `NoShortcut`. `ID` and `Relationship` are hidden. `Name` and `Tags` are entity-level, so `.Name` is the entity's name string and tags use the tag methods. `Script` is `NoShortcut`: `GetScript(name?)` and `GetScripts()` return the instances (§11.2), and `GetComponent("Script")` returns the component proxy. **Entity members take precedence.** Registration asserts at startup that no shortcut collides with an `Entity` method or property, so a future component cannot shadow one silently.

### 11.5 Full API surface
| Module / type | Members |
|---|---|
| `Script`, `Field` | `Script.Define<T>(name, class: T) -> T` (§11.2); `Field.Number(default?, options?)`, `Field.Integer`, `Field.Bool`, `Field.String`, `Field.Vector`, `Field.Color`, `Field.Quat`, `Field.Entity()`, `Field.Asset(type)`, `Field.Enum(values, default?)`, `Field.Array(fieldKind)`; options `{Min, Max, Step, Tooltip}` |
| `Entity` (userdata) | `.ID` (hex string), `.Name` (rw); `:IsValid()`, `:IsActive()` (effective), `:IsActiveSelf()`, `:SetActive(active)`, `:HasTag(tag)`, `:AddTag(tag)`, `:RemoveTag(tag)`, `:GetTags()`, `:HasComponent(name)`, `:GetComponent(name)` (overloaded per component name in d.luau), `:AddComponent(name, values?)`, `:RemoveComponent(name)`, `:GetScript(name?)` (the instance table of the first script slot, or of the first slot whose behaviour is named `name`; nil when there is none; typed `any`, §11.2), `:GetScripts()` (the live instances of the entity's script slots, in slot order), `:GetParent()`, `:SetParent(parent?, keepWorld?)`, `:GetChildren()`, `:FindChild(name, recursive?)`, `:GetWorldBounds() -> (vector?, vector?)` (render AABB min/max of this entity's `MeshRenderer`, nil without one), `:Destroy()`; shortcut properties `.Transform`, `.RigidBody`, … per the rule in §11.4 (nil when absent); `==` compares UUIDs |
| Component proxies | every scriptable registry field of every component, read/write; plus methods below |
| `Transform` | fields `Translation`, `Rotation`, `Scale`, `EulerAngles`, `WorldPosition` (rw), `WorldRotation` (rw), `WorldScale` (r), `RenderPosition` (r), `RenderRotation` (r) (interpolated, §5.2); `:Teleport(position?, rotation?)` (world pose without interpolation), `:Forward()`, `:Right()`, `:Up()`, `:LookAt(target, up?)`, `:Translate(delta, space?)`, `:Rotate(eulerDegrees, space?)`, `:TransformPoint(p)`, `:InverseTransformPoint(p)`, `:TransformDirection(d)` |
