### 11.6 Creating, destroying, spawning
Immediate creation and deferred destruction as defined in §5.7. `Scene.Instantiate` uses the shared prefab path (§5.5) with a root ID from the session's seeded generator. `AddComponent(name, values)` validates values against the registry before adding.

### 11.7 Error reporting
Every callback runs under `Lua::ProtectedCall` with an error handler that walks the stack with `lua_getinfo` (at most 32 frames) and maps each frame's chunk to its authored project path and line. Every task and test-case resume goes through `Lua::ProtectedResume`, which takes the traceback from the dead thread's stack after `lua_resume` returns an error status; `lua_resume` takes no error handler, and the errored thread keeps its frames. Both produce a structured `ScriptError`:
```json
{ "id": 17, "kind": "runtime", "script": "Assets/Scripts/Board.luau", "line": 88, "column": 0,
  "message": "attempt to index nil with 'Transform'", "callback": "OnFixedUpdate",
  "entity": { "id": "8f3a2c1d9e4b7a60", "name": "Game" }, "slot": 0, "tick": 412, "count": 1,
  "traceback": [ { "script": "Assets/Scripts/Board.luau", "line": 88, "function": "LockPiece" } ] }
```
`kind` ∈ {`compile`, `type`, `runtime`, `timeout`, `memory`}; `type` is published when a hot reload is refused because `Scripting.BlockPlayOnTypeErrors` is set and the reimported script has type errors, which keeps the running code (ADR 0022 decision 15). An error with an entity names its behaviour's `slot` in the entity's Script list (for an evaluation, the slot it bound `self` to; ADR 0031 decision 17); the slot is not part of the deduplication key. A native fault (§11.11: `callback` `NativeStep`, `script` `native:<System>`) has no behaviour: its `slot` is 0 and names no Script slot, and its entity may hold no Script component (ADR 0031, "Merge with M19"). An error from Luau embedded in another file (a replay's `Expect`) also carries `jsonPointer`, the location of that source (`/Expect/0/Luau`), and its `line` and `column` count in the decoded Luau (ADR 0019 decision 5). Errors are deduplicated by (script, jsonPointer, line, message) with a `count` of their occurrences, the context and `tick` being the latest occurrence's (`tick` is the session's tick its callback ran in, as `Time.GetSessionTick()` reads it there, `Time.GetTick()` too in a session whose world never paused (§5.6): in the fixed step the zero-based index of the tick being run, in the frame phase the ticks completed; ADR 0038 friction F16), logged to the `Script` logger, appended to the script error stream (`script.errors`, `_meta`, console, `EventLog`, `Test.GetScriptErrors`; a stream keeps the 256 distinct errors with the latest occurrences, §11.1, and `script.errors` reports `evicted: true` when an error newer than its `since` cursor was evicted), and the faulting **instance is disabled** (no further callbacks, its tasks cancelled, until a hot reload of its script; whatever `Scripting.PauseOnError` says), so one bad script cannot spam at 60 Hz while others keep running, and each faulting instance adds one to its error's `count`. A failed external evaluation (`script.eval`, `play.waitFor`, a replay `Expect`), even one addressed to an entity, is not a callback of that instance: it is never attributed to the behaviour's file, never disables it, cancels its tasks or pauses play. A failed `play.waitFor` predicate or replay `Expect` is reported and logged the same way as a callback's error; a failed `script.eval` is the caller's own error (ADR 0038, friction F01): it is logged and answered with its located error (`scriptError`), but never appended to the script error stream or the `EventLog`, and its log entry takes no part in the response's `_meta` diagnostics (friction F13), so `script.errors` and `_meta` list only the game's errors (one that stopped the VM, a hard memory breach, is the game's and is published). With `Scripting.PauseOnError` (default true) the editor pauses play at the first runtime error so an agent lands on the frozen state. The Runtime logs, disables the instance and continues. Test runs never pause, in any mode: the runner owns time, so Editor, Release and Dist runs observe the same audio and interpolation after an error. In test runs an error in a behaviour is recorded for the suite and fails the running case unless that case expects it (`Test.ExpectScriptError`); an error inside a case body fails that case at the error's location. `Test.Fail`/`Test.Skip` called from a behaviour end the running case without disabling the behaviour.

### 11.8 Hot reload
Edit mode: a changed script is recompiled and re-checked (and every script that requires it is re-extracted, §7.5); the inspector refreshes the field schema. Play mode (editor only; lockstep, replay, recording and test sessions defer reloads, §7.5): if compilation fails the old code keeps running and a `compile` error is raised. If the re-check finds type errors in a script of the reload chain while the type gate applies (`Scripting.BlockPlayOnTypeErrors` in ordinary play; always in a test session, because type errors always block test runs, §11.9), the old code keeps running and a `type` error is raised (`EditorPlayController::CheckReloadTypes`, ADR 0022 decision 15). On success:
1. **Behaviours** re-execute and **the class table's contents are replaced in place**. Instances' metatable is the class table, so every instance gets the new methods while its state survives; new fields get their defaults; `OnHotReload(self)` runs if defined. An instance that has no table to keep (its module top faulted at creation, or a memory fault dropped it) is recreated from its field defaults and overrides and restarts its lifecycle instead: `OnCreate` now (before any surviving instance's `OnHotReload`), `OnStart` at the next start flush.
2. **Modules** (plain `require`d scripts) re-execute. If the old and new results are both tables, the old table's contents are replaced in place with the new ones, so every holder of the table sees the new functions. Then **every dependent** (transitively, in dependency order: modules first, then behaviours) re-executes the same way. Locals that a dependent captured from the module (`local new = Board.new`) are therefore re-bound. If a module returns a non-table value, its dependents are re-executed to pick it up. The VM's require cache is updated to the patched table.
3. The reload is one step: a failure anywhere in the chain (compile or top-level error) rolls back to the previous code for the whole chain and raises one error naming the failing script.

The editor queues published script handles and processes them at its safe point after UI, RPC and batch dispatch have returned. When new publications arrived since the last safe point, it first finishes their dependent imports; a chain kept waiting never blocks later frames on unrelated imports. It deduplicates overlapping chains and reports failed imports without replacing the running code: a chain waits while any script `ScriptEngine::GetReloadChain` names (the changed script plus the loaded modules and attached behaviours that require it) has a failed latest import, until that script imports again. Project scripts outside the live chain, such as a test suite requiring the module, never hold it back. A failed import is reported as a `compile` error at the failing file, line and column: the import attempt records its own located failure (syntax, load-time extraction, an unresolved require) beside the checker's findings. Ending a deferred session drains the released import chain before a subsequent Start can read its assets (ADR 0019 decision 10).

`Test.ReloadScript(asset)` (EditorOnly) triggers the same path synchronously from a test, type gate included (a refused reload raises the `type` error's message at the call), so `Callbacks.scene` asserts `OnHotReload` in the editor run. Tests: "HotReload: instance state survives", "HotReload: editing a required module updates dependents", "HotReload: a failing dependent rolls back the chain", "HotReload: deferred while lockstep owns time".

### 11.9 Static type checking
`ScriptTypeChecker` (EditorCore and Tests only; the Runtime links only the VM, Luau's parser and, outside Dist, its compiler) wraps `Luau::Frontend` with `SolverMode::New`, a `FileResolver` over the project VFS (the same resolution as runtime `require`), a `ConfigResolver` reading `.luaurc` (default `--!strict`; nested files apply from the project root down, so the nearest directory's file wins whatever the directory names), `registerBuiltinGlobals`, `loadDefinitionFile` with the definitions the live script API registry generates in memory (`ScriptApiRegistry::GenerateDefinitions`, loaded under the chunk name `Engine.d.luau`), then `freeze`. A checker does that once per frontend: it keeps the frontends it prepared and leases each to one check at a time, which sets its own file and configuration resolvers; a completed check clears every module and source before the frontend is leased again, and a check that throws drops it, so findings never depend on reuse and sequential checks load the definitions once per checker (ADR 0041 decision 1). Its configuration is a snapshot of the `.luaurc` files from the project root down (`ScriptTypeChecker::CaptureConfiguration` lists every directory under `Assets/`, so a `.luaurc` added to a new directory is seen). Only present files enter the checker's environment hash, which a cached import's check must match, and the editor's refresh hash, so a new directory without a `.luaurc` keeps the checker and every script's check, while a `.luaurc` added, changed or removed replaces the checker and checks every script again (ADR 0041 decision 2). The committed `Resources/Scripting/Engine.d.luau` is never read at run time, so a stale or missing copy cannot change a diagnostic, and `GenerateDocs.py --check` keeps it byte-equal to the registry (ADR 0025). Calls are wrapped in `try`/`catch (const Luau::InternalCompilerError&)`. Diagnostics are `{file, line, column, endLine, endColumn, code, severity, message}` (1-based); syntax errors carry `SCRIPT_COMPILE_ERROR` and every other finding `SCRIPT_TYPE_ERROR`, Luau's lint warnings included (the checker runs Luau's lints, every one enabled by default), which have severity `Warning`: `script.check`'s `passed` counts only errors, while the games suite fails a game on any diagnostic (§15.1 T5). A missing or misspelled required module is a located finding; only infrastructure failures (I/O, permissions) fail a check. It runs on save, in `script.check` and in `project.validate`; `Editor --headless --check-scripts` runs it from the command line. CI runs it through the stages that refuse type errors, the feature and export suites over FeatureTest (test runs and exports fail on any type error), and through the `DocExamples` unit case for the documentation. Type errors always block export and test runs; they block Play only when `Scripting.BlockPlayOnTypeErrors` is true (default false, so agents can iterate on partial scripts while seeing diagnostics in `_meta`). Analysis has no wall-clock limit and no cancellation token (Luau's `moduleTimeLimitSec` and `cancellationToken` stay unset), so a check's findings never depend on how loaded the machine is. User-defined type functions (`type function`, `export type function`) are refused before analysis with a located `SCRIPT_TYPE_ERROR` at each declaration's name, in the checked script and in every module it requires (a refused module never reaches the frontend): Luau runs their bodies as Luau in its analysis VM, whose only interrupt is that time limit or token, so a looping body would hang the check, and with it imports, `script.check`, `project.validate` and test discovery. Nothing else in analysis runs user code; Luau's complexity limits, which count work rather than time, bound the rest of every check and report what they cut short as a located `SCRIPT_TYPE_ERROR` (ADR 0022 "Integration"). All Analysis API use is confined to one `.cpp`, pinned to the vendored release.

`Engine.d.luau` is generated from the registries using Luau 0.741's current definition syntax (`declare class` is being removed upstream). Members are sorted by name, each after its description comment; methods are function-typed members, and only the overloaded `GetComponent` uses the `function` form. An excerpt (most members left out):
```lua skip="an excerpt of the generated declaration file, not a script"
-- A UUID and scene generation identifying an entity; no native address is exposed.
declare extern type Entity with
	function GetComponent(self, name: "Transform"): Transform?
	function GetComponent(self, name: "RigidBody"): RigidBody?
	-- Get the instance of the first script slot whose behaviour has this name, or of the first slot without a name; nil when there is none. [All modes; Runtime|Test; pure/read]
	GetScript: (self: Entity, name: string?) -> any
	-- Get this entity's render mesh world AABB; nil without a mesh. [All modes; Runtime|Test; pure/read]
	GetWorldBounds: (self: Entity) -> (vector?, vector?)
	-- The immutable 16-digit hexadecimal UUID. [All modes; Runtime|Test; pure/read]
	ID: string
	-- Whether this identity still names a live entity in this scene. [All modes; Runtime|Test; pure/read]
	IsValid: (self: Entity) -> boolean
	-- The entity name; a written name is UTF-8 without NUL and at most 256 bytes. [All modes; Runtime|Test; pure/read; setter mutates]
	Name: string
	-- The entity's RigidBody component, or nil when absent. [All modes; Runtime|Test; pure/read]
	RigidBody: RigidBody?
	-- The entity's Transform component, which every entity has. [All modes; Runtime|Test; pure/read]
	Transform: Transform
end
-- Behaviour class registration.
declare Script: {
	-- Authenticate a behaviour class and return the exact same table. [All modes; LoadTime|Runtime|Test; pure/read]
	Define: <T>(name: string, class: T) -> T,
}
```
`GenerateDocs.py --check` fails CI when the committed file is stale, and every Luau example in the documentation (`Docs/*.md`, `Docs/Reference/*.md`, `AGENTS.md`, the project and template `AGENTS.md` files and the skills with their reference pages; `Docs/Decisions/` excluded) is extracted and type-checked in CI by the unit test "DocExamples: every Luau example in the docs type-checks", with the fence attributes `path=`, `prelude=` and `skip=` of ADR 0022 decision 14 (the project modules an example requires, such as `Board`, are provided as stubs under `Tests/Data/TypeChecker/DocExamples/`). The same examples must be free of lint warnings ("DocExamples: every Luau example in the docs is free of lint warnings"), since a builder copies them into scripts that the games suite checks, except a game's own `AGENTS.md` (`Projects/*/AGENTS.md`, `Tests/Projects/*/AGENTS.md`), whose fences only the type check reads: `script.check` never reads the notes, and their builder has no tool that lints a fence (ADR 0027 decision 5, C1). TypeChecker fixtures (`Tests/Data/TypeChecker/`) pin the expected diagnostics for the three templates, a behaviour declaring every `Field` kind, the `GetScript` cast idiom, a test suite, and seeded mistakes (an optional passed to a non-optional parameter, a member added to a sealed table).

### 11.10 Test scripts and the test runner
**Shape.** A test script (`*.test.luau`, created from the `Test` template) is a module that returns one suite:
```lua path=Assets/Tests/Tetris.test.luau
--!strict
local Board = require("../Scripts/Board")
local GameScript = require("../Scripts/Game")

return Test.Suite("Tetris", function()
	Test.Case("four lines clear for 800 points", function()
		local board = Board.New()
		board:FillRows(0, 3, 4)   -- rows 0-3 full except column 4
		board:Place("I", 4, 0, 1)
		Test.ExpectEqual(board:ClearLines(), 4)
		Test.ExpectEqual(Board.Score(4, 1), 800)
	end)

	Test.Case("hard drop locks the piece", function()
		local game = Scene.FindByName("Game")
		Test.Expect(game ~= nil, "Main.scene has a Game entity")
		local state = (game :: Entity):GetScript() :: GameScript.Game
		local locked = state.LockedCount
		Test.InjectAction("HardDrop", "Tap")
		Test.WaitTicks(2)
		Test.ExpectEqual(state.LockedCount, locked + 1)
	end, { TimeoutTicks = 120 })
end)
```
- `Test.Suite(name, body, options?)` is a pure constructor (available in the load-time VM, §11.2) returning `{Name, Body, Options}`, so the module top stays side-effect free. The importer classifies the script as a `TestSuite`. A TestSuite cannot be attached to an entity (`SCRIPT_NOT_A_BEHAVIOUR`).
- Suite options accept `CaseTimeoutTicks` (positive integer) as the default for cases without their own `TimeoutTicks`; otherwise the project's `Testing.CaseTimeoutTicks` applies. Unknown options are errors. `Test.ExpectScriptError(pattern, withinTicks)` claims one nonfatal occurrence observed during the current case, preserving logs/counts; unmatched faults fail the case, and setup/teardown, fatal and case-body faults cannot be claimed. Its pattern uses Luau string-pattern rules. These host and option details are recorded in ADR 0019.
- `Test.Case(name, fn, options?)` only registers a case. It is valid only while the runner executes a suite body, and raises `Test.Case outside Test.Suite` anywhere else.
- `Test.Fail` and `Test.Skip` called in a suite body, where no case is active, raise a catchable script error and end nothing; like every call, they are counted on entry. FeatureTest covers both for gate 2 this way, through `pcall` in a suite body, because it allows no failed or skipped case row (ADR 0022 decision 4). The `Test` module exists only in test runs; in normal play every member except `Suite` raises `Test is only available in test runs`.

**Binding to scenes.** The project's `Testing` settings list suites and replays:
- `Suites: [{Script, Scene?, Parameters?, Isolation?, Clock?, Overrides?, ExpectQuit?, Modes?, Locale?}]`. `Scene` is the scene the suite runs in. If it is omitted, the suite runs in an **empty scene** (no entities), which is right for pure-logic suites such as Board tests. `Parameters` become `Scene.GetLoadParameters()`. `Isolation` is `"Suite"` (default: cases share one scene instance, in order) or `"Case"` (the scene is reloaded before each case). `Clock` is a list of frame deltas that selects `ScriptedClock` (§4.2) instead of lockstep `ManualClock`. `Overrides` holds `{CallbackBudgetMs?, MemoryLimitMB?, PauseOnError?}`, applied exactly (no Dist minimum) for that suite; a script error never pauses a test run, so `PauseOnError` has no effect on its time in any mode (§11.7). `ExpectQuit` is the exit code the suite must end with through `Application.Quit`. `Modes` is a subset of `["Editor", "Release", "Dist"]` (default: all). `Locale` (M38, ADR 0055 decision 6) is the locale the suite's sessions start in, empty (the default) or a tag: empty takes the run's locale (`test.run {locale}`, the Runtime's `--locale` with `--feature-test`), else the project's `Localization.Locale`. A project lists a strings suite once per locale; an entry that names a locale is reported as `<Name> (<Locale>)` in every row and against the filter, and every suite row reports the `locale` its sessions started in (a replay row its header's).
- Suites and replays play saved scene files, never the editor's open scenes, whichever is active: `test.run` refuses while any open scene that a selected suite or replay plays has unsaved changes (§13.5), and while a test run owns the editor no open scene can be activated or closed (ADR 0031 decisions 13 and 14). A suite reads one behaviour of an entity with several scripts through `GetScript(name)` or `GetScripts()` (§11.2).
- `Replays: [globs]` (`.replay` files, §6.7). `CaseTimeoutTicks` (default 600) and `SuiteTickLimit` (default 36,000) bound every case and suite. `CoverageGates` (default false) opts the project into coverage recording and the per-mode gates of §15.6 in its unfiltered, non-recording runs (`Projects/FeatureTest` sets it; ADR 0022 decision 3).

A scripted clock also uses the current case's effective `TimeoutTicks` as a limit on consecutive completed frames with no fixed step. Frame callbacks run before the check, allowing a finite pause to recover; any stepped frame resets the counter. Reaching the limit times out the case at its source location, cancels its thread and capture, and closes the suite. Tick counts and tick budgets still measure actual simulation ticks. Frame deltas may be 0, but an authored clock whose deltas are all 0 is rejected when the settings load (ADR 0019 decision 10, ADR 0022 decision 9).

**Execution** (`Engine/Testing/FeatureTestRunner`, shared by every entry point). For each suite in list order:
1. Start a fresh `PlaySession` of the suite's scene, in test mode with the session seed (the project's `Simulation.Seed` XOR the scene's `Seed`; an empty scene's is 0) and lockstep `ManualClock` (or the suite's `ScriptedClock`), and apply its overrides. Run session setup (`OnCreate`, `OnStart`).
2. Call the suite body in the play VM to collect cases, in declaration order.
3. Run the cases **sequentially**. Each case body runs as its own thread (`lua_newthread`, resumed at step 4 of every tick, §5.7), so `Test.WaitTicks`/`WaitUntil` work. A case ends when its thread returns (passed, unless an `Expect*` failed), raises (error, located at the raising line), calls `Test.Fail` (failed) or `Test.Skip` (skipped), or exceeds its tick timeout (timeout, located at the line where it was waiting). Gameplay code may end the running case with `Test.Fail` or `Test.Skip` too; a case thread, or a task a behaviour spawned (which the case does not own, and which is cancelled), never runs past the call, even inside `pcall`. A lifecycle callback is not yieldable, so there the signal is raised as a script error that unwinds to the nearest `pcall`; the case's outcome stays latched either way. `Expect*` failures are recorded with the caller's file and line, and the case continues so one run reports every failed expectation.
4. With `Isolation: "Case"`, the scene restarts before the next case. After the last case the session is destroyed. **The scene is always restarted between suites.** A case during which a transition is requested (by the case or by a game script) must return in the requesting tick, before the VM replacement at that frame's end, which on a ScriptedClock comes right after that tick as in lockstep (ADR 0038 decision 15); a still-suspended case becomes a located error. Suite isolation re-collects the same ordered case identities/options in the new VM and continues at the next case. Changed collection is an error; no coroutine survives a destroyed VM (ADR 0019 decision 6).
5. `Application.Quit(code)` during a suite ends that suite immediately with the event `quit(code)`. It passes only if `ExpectQuit` equals `code`; otherwise the running case fails. `ExpectQuit` below 0 (the default -1) means the suite must not quit at all, so even `Application.Quit(-1)` fails. A quit first raised by final teardown is also reported and compared with `ExpectQuit`; the first request is classified exactly once. `Debug.Break` is a counted no-op in test runs.
6. The suite and run tick limits stop stepping where they are reached. A case still running then times out; a case that already finished earlier in the same frame keeps its result, and selected cases the limit leaves unrun are reported once as a `<tick limit>` timeout row of the suite.

`Test.Screenshot(name)` captures through the host (the editor writes each capture to a new PNG in its automation output directory, the Runtime to `user://TestResults/<name>.png`), so the runner bounds a suite to 256 calls (`MaxScriptTestScreenshotsPerSuite`, counted whatever the host's outcome). A later call in the suite reaches no host and raises a located error naming the limit; unhandled, it fails its case like any script error, and the run goes on and publishes its report as usual.

Every suite and replay session owns simulation audio time for its whole lifetime (the host sets `PlaySessionSpecification::OwnsAudioTime`); the runner checks the session the host returned and fails the suite's setup when an engine exists and the session does not own its time. Each suite and replay session starts from the host's test-run cursor baseline (`Normal`), so a cursor mode a suite sets never reaches the next one, whatever the order or filter.

Replays then run one by one, each in a fresh session started from its header (§6.7): events are applied by tick, every `Expect` is evaluated at its tick (bytecode from the cooked replay in exported runs), every state-hash checkpoint is compared as playback reaches its tick (the first that differs ends the replay with a failed `Checkpoint@<tick>` row located at `/Checkpoints/<index>/StateHash`, naming both hashes), and the final state hash is compared with the header's `FinalStateHash`: a replay that ends without stopping, and either has no `Expect` entries or ends with another hash, gets a `FinalStateHash` case row, passed when the hash matches and failed (`expected <hash>, observed <hash>` at `/FinalStateHash`) when it differs, so a hash mismatch always fails the replay. Both failures' messages add the divergence hint, since the replay plays with its recording's input: the world differs from the recording (a serialized component of the scene, the look's included, a script, the game's native module, an asset or the engine changed since it was recorded, or the play is not deterministic); re-record it with `test.run {record}`. A passing `FinalStateHash` row (the name is kept, ADR 0026 friction S3-04) therefore also means that every checkpoint matched, and the replay's suite entry counts them (`checkpointsChecked`, the failed one included) and names the tick of a checkpoint that differed (`failedCheckpointTick`, 0 when none did). A replay that cannot load, start or play becomes failed `replay:<path>` rows (`<replay>`), and gameplay that quits or stops fatally before the replay's `FinalTick` is a failed replay (`<stopped>`, with the tick reached and the reason) rather than an error of the whole run; the run continues with the next replay.

Replay cancellation drops future authored events before releasing the session's input/time lease. Already-applied input remains at the paused boundary: an applied Tap retains its next-tick release, and held buttons/axes remain until subsequent input or `input.inject releaseAll`. Independent input is preserved. The player validates all events before starting and queues them only at their execution tick (ADR 0019 decision 10).

**One result schema** for `FeatureTestRunner`, `test.run`, `Editor --run-tests` and exported `--feature-test`, written to `bin/TestResults/<run>.json` and JUnit:
`{suite, case, status: passed|failed|error|timeout|skipped|quit, message, file, line, ticks}` per case at least, plus `jsonPointer` (embedded Luau), `failures` (every `Expect*` failure and unexpected script error of the row) and, on a quit row, `quitCode` and `quitExpected` (ADR 0019) (replays use `suite = "replay:<path>"` and `case = "Expect@<tick>"` or `"FinalStateHash"`), plus per-suite `{suite, scene, mode, ticks, breaks, scriptErrors, finalStateHash, checkpointsChecked, failedCheckpointTick}` (the last two for replays, 0 for script suites; additive, ADR 0026 friction S3-04), the run's coverage report (§15.6), its `counts` (the rows by status: `total`, `passed`, `failed`, `error`, `timeout`, `skipped`, `quit`) and `failedCases` (`"<suite>/<case>"` of each row that fails the run: failed, error, timeout, or a quit that was not expected or has failures; in row order, at most 20). The reports always hold the coverage counters; `test.run`'s RPC result keeps the `coverage` object with its `registryFingerprint` and `gates` but leaves `coverage.counters` out (an empty list) unless they are asked for (`coverage: true`, or the project's `Testing.CoverageGates`), so an ordinary run's result stays inline with its pass/fail counts and failing cases (ADR 0026, frictions S1-02 and S3-10). A `test.run {record}` that wrote its replay reports it, in the result and the JSON report, as `recording {path, formatVersion, ticks, events, checkpoints, finalStateHash, inputCheck: {ran, divergedAtTick}, expectations, warnings}` (`divergedAtTick`: where the input check's run without input first differed, at the first checkpoint whose hash differed or at the final tick; `ran` false for a recording without input events; `expectations`: the count of `test.run {expect}` expectations written, each verified with the recording's input; `warnings`: the input check's final-hash warning, `MakeFinalHashIndependentWarning`, when its run without input differed only at checkpoints and reached the recorded final hash; ADR 0030 decisions 6 and 3); `recording` is null for every other run, a refused recording included, and `recordingPath` stays (additive, ADR 0026 friction S3-03). Names and messages come from scripts, bounded as §11.1 says (a suite or case name at most 256 bytes; a message at most 8 KiB of the script's text, with authored locations, before the sanitizing below, which can expand one control byte into the six-byte escape `\u00XX`; at most 32 script-driven failures per row, the last then counting any more as `[truncated: <n> more failures]`, and 1,024 per suite), so the runner makes every reported text valid for JSON and XML: invalid UTF-8 bytes (and U+FFFE/U+FFFF) become U+FFFD and control characters other than tab, line feed and carriage return become the visible text `\u00XX`. **`filter`** (in `test.run`, `--run-tests --filter`) is a case-insensitive substring matched against `"<suite>/<case>"`, so `"Tetris"` selects a suite and `"Tetris/hard drop"` one case. Replays match on their path.

The runner is part of the `Testing` module, which stays in Dist, so exported Release and Dist runtimes execute exactly the same suites and replays (§14.4). The test template, a documentation example and a TypeChecker fixture keep this shape type-checked.

### 11.11 Native gameplay modules
A game may hold one native C++ module, the `.cpp` and `.h` files below `<Game>/Native/` (M19, Windows only; ADR 0030 decisions 26 to 35). Luau stays the gameplay language of §11.1 to §11.10; the module is for simulation code that needs C++, and both run in one session.
- **Interface.** `Engine/Native/NativeApi.h` is the one engine header a module includes (served by `docs.get` as `native/NativeApi.h`, §13.10): header-only, standard library and glm only, so the module links no engine library. One source names the registration function with `ENGINE_NATIVE_MODULE`; it registers component types (data on entities), resource types (one value per play session) and systems through `INativeRegistrar`. A type is a trivially copyable, standard-layout struct naming itself with `NativeTypeName`; its reflected fields have the kinds of `NativeFieldKind` (bool, int32, uint32, float, the glm vectors and quaternion, linear colours, `NativeEntity`, an enum class over int32), each with a description and optional bounds, unit and `RenamedFrom`. Members it does not register are neither saved nor hashed.
- **Registration** (`Native/NativeModule.h`, `BuildNativeModuleTypes`): the module's interface version must be `NativeApiVersion`, and the registration is validated as a whole (PascalCase names unique within their kind, descriptions, sizes, alignments and non-overlapping field layouts, bounds, enum entries, defaults each field accepts, the limits); the first broken rule refuses the module with `Validation` naming the type, field or system, as does an exception that escapes the registration (§4.6 item 8). The result, `NativeModuleTypes`, is immutable and lives beside the frozen `TypeRegistry`, not in it, since a module comes and goes with the editor's hot reload: native components have no script proxy, inspector drawer or `component.schema` (`native.status` gives each type's JSON Schema). Its layout hash changes exactly when a type's canonical JSON can.
- **Components in scenes** (§6.2, `Native/NativeComponents.h`): a native component lives as its JSON among the entity's preserved components, so the serializer, the play copy, undo snapshots and prefabs carry it unchanged and an editor without the module loses nothing. With the module loaded it is made canonical when a scene opens (a new tab's too), when the module loads or reloads (in every open scene, M20), on `native.setComponents` and when a Play session starts: values migrate by field name (a renamed field through `RenamedFrom`, a member no field is named after dropped with `NATIVE_FIELD_DROPPED`, a value that does not convert reset with `NATIVE_FIELD_RESET`); a value its type rejects is `NATIVE_COMPONENT_INVALID`, kept as written, and keeps a Play session of its scene from starting; a component the module does not register is kept with `NATIVE_COMPONENT_UNREGISTERED`. The warnings are errors under `--strict`. Automation's scene reads report them as the scene holds them, unchecked against the loaded module (`native.getComponents` reads them through it): `scene.tree` lists their names after the built-in components, `entity.get` (`all`, the default) and `scene.query`'s `select: ["all"]` carry their JSON, and a `Native.<Name>` in `entity.get`'s `components` or in `scene.query`'s `where.component` and `select` names one. Only `native.setComponents` writes them: a `Native.<Name>` in `entity.create`'s, `entity.update`'s or `prefab.instantiate`'s `components`, or in `entity.update`'s `removeComponents`, is refused (`InvalidArgument`, `MakeNativeComponentWriteError`) with a hint naming `native.setComponents`, so `entity.get`'s components sent back are not answered with did-you-mean names of built-in components. A script's component lookup of a `Native.<Name>` fails with `NotFound` (a native component has no script proxy), whose hint names `native.getComponents` (scripts and test suites check the built-in state their systems write).
- **NativeStep** (§5.7 step 4a, `Session/NativeWorld.h`): a Play session with a module owns a `NativeWorld` for its whole life, `Scene.Load` included (Simulate has none). Each system gets an `INativeStepContext`: the tick and fixed delta; `Query` over the effectively active entities that hold a component, in canonical order; component and resource data at fixed addresses until the system returns (a component's data is read from its JSON the first time a system asks for it in the step, with the migration above, since only the starting scene is canonical); entity creation and destruction with §5.7's semantics and entity limit; local transforms written as a script's Transform write in `OnFixedUpdate`; the latched step view of the project's actions (an action the project does not define reads as up and 0 and logs one error per session); the session's Random stream; DetMath; the log (`native:<System>`, at most 1,024 lines per step). After each system every value it changed is checked against its type and put back when it is rejected; when the phase ends the changed, added and removed components are written back to the scene. A value its type rejects, read or written, and an exception that escapes a system (§4.6 item 8) stop the session fatally (`PlaySession::GetFatalError`, naming the system, published to the session's error stream as a runtime error with `script` `native:<System>`, `callback` `NativeStep`, the faulting entity when there is one and `slot` 0, which names no behaviour, §11.7); a crash in native code is not caught.
- **State and determinism.** Resources start at their defaults and keep their values across `Scene.Load`; the state hash's native block holds them (§5.1). Native code is simulation code (§1.3, §4.12): it is compiled with the first-party settings, checked by the determinism lint, reads time only as ticks, randomness only from the session's stream and input only from the latched step view, and keeps no mutable state of its own (every variable of static or thread storage duration is const or constexpr), since the editor keeps a module's library loaded across sessions while each exported Runtime starts fresh. A native component's data round-trips through its JSON once per step that touches it (an accepted limit, `Docs/Backlog.md`).

### 11.12 Visual scripting graphs
A graph is one behaviour drawn as nodes and links (M24, `Docs/Decisions/0035-m24-contract.md` decisions 2 to 9 and 24): a `.graph` source (its format is §6's) that `GraphImporter` transpiles to Luau and compiles through this chapter's pipeline, so it is a Script asset of the importer `Graph`, its cooked artifact a `ScriptData` like a `.luau` source's, and a script slot, the script engine, hot reload, the paks and Dist run it as any behaviour. Dist runs its bytecode and needs no transpiler: the graph code lives in `AssetPipeline/Graph/`, which the Runtime never links.
- **The node library** (`GraphNodeLibrary`) grows from the frozen script API: `Create` derives a kind from every member available in every run mode and at run time whose canonical signature is one function type of modelled types (`Event.<Callback>` from the Behaviour callbacks, `Call.<Group>.<Member>` from functions, methods and constructors, `Get`/`Set` from properties, component proxy fields and record aliases' fields, `Const` from constants), so a binding adds its node and changes it with itself; generics, overload intersections and function-typed members have none. Pins are typed (`GraphPinType`: Luau's numbers, booleans, strings, vectors, Colors, Quats, Entities, AssetRefs, a registered enum's choices, any other named type as Object, tables and unions as Any); a `T?` output may give nil and feeds only an optional input or Any, `Flow.IfNotNil` turning it into a value every input takes. The built-ins are the flow nodes (Branch, Sequence, ForRange, ForEach, Delay, IfNotNil), the instance's members (`Self.Entity`, `Self.Get.<Name>`, `Self.Set.<Name>`, and M39's `Self.Instance`, the instance itself), the members of any value (M39: `Script.Get`, `Script.Set` and `Script.Call`, which read, write and call a member of a behaviour instance or a table named by a string, as Any) and the number, comparison, logic, vector and text operators. A member registered with `Mutates` false that returns a value, a getter, a constant and an operator is pure (evaluated where each statement reads it); every other node is a statement with `In` and `Then`.
- **Methods and returns** (M39, `Docs/Decisions/0056-m39-graphs-behaviours.md` decisions 3 to 5): a graph declares methods (§6.11), each run by its `Method.<Name>` event nodes (their outputs the parameters, typed by kind) and ended by its `Return.<Name>` nodes (a statement with `In`, no exec output, and a `Value` typed by the result when there is one), graph-dependent kinds like `Self.*`; and every Behaviour callback with a result (the `OnUi*` ones, `boolean?`) has a `Return.<Callback>` kind, whose `Value` true consumes the UI event. A script calls a graph's method on its instance (`entity:GetScript("Rune"):Damaged(hit)`, or `Script.Call`), in the caller's callback and phase. A `Return` ends the function that runs it, Luau's own return: later statements of its flow and later event nodes of its function do not run; it is reached only from its own function's event nodes and never through `Flow.Delay`'s `Later` flow (`GRAPH_INVALID`). Shared behaviour is reached through a behaviour instance (`Call.Scene.FindByPath`, `Flow.IfNotNil`, `Call.Entity.GetScript`, then `Script.Get` or `Script.Call`): a graph still requires no module.
- **Validation** (`ValidateGraph`, beyond the document's own `ValidateGraphStructure`): every kind resolves, every literal names a data input and fits its type, every link joins an output to a compatible input, a data input and an exec output take one link, no data or exec cycle, a Quat literal is no zero quaternion (which `Quat.New` refuses), and, once every other issue is Incomplete, no statement's code starts more than 64 blocks deep in the transpiled text and the text holds at most 8 MiB (measured by laying the text out as the transpiler does, the limits constants they share in `AssetPipeline/Private/GraphTextLimits.h`, the layout stopping at the size limit, so a graph transpiles exactly when it validates); and, as Incomplete issues the edit methods accept and the import refuses, every required input without a default is linked or set, a statement's or event's output is read only by statements it dominates in the flow from the events (computed over all events at once, in topological order), `Flow.IfNotNil`'s `Result` only by statements that its `True` flow alone leads to, where its value is not nil, and a loop's (`Flow.ForRange`'s, `Flow.ForEach`'s) `Index` or `Element` into an input that needs a value (neither optional nor Any) only by statements that its `Body` flow alone leads to, since on its `Completed` flow and after it they are nil when the loop ran zero times (ADR 0035's milestone review). `FindUnreachableGraphNodes` lists the statements no event reaches. The issues become `GRAPH_INVALID` and `GRAPH_UNREACHABLE_NODE` (§13.7).
- **The transpiler** (`TranspileGraph`) writes one strict-clean Luau text per graph, a pure function of the document, the library and the path, byte-identical in every configuration: `--!strict`, the generated-from comment, `Graph.Fields`, `Graph.RunsWhileWorldPaused = true` when the graph opts in (M39), `OnCreate` (which creates the live-value table, then the variables), one function per other callback with event nodes in byte-wise order, one function per method in name order (M39; its parameters the locals `p_<Name>`, so none shadows a global or a generated local), and `Script.Define`. M39's text: `Script.Get` is `(<object> :: any)[<member>]`; `Script.Set` and `Script.Call` bind their object to the local `o<Id>: any`, the call `o<Id>:<Method>(...)` for a literal method name that is a member's name (`IsGraphIdentifier`) and `o<Id>[<method>](o<Id>, ...)` otherwise, its first result cast to any; a `Return` is `return` in a `do ... end` block of its own; a merge whose flow reaches a `Return` is a `flow<Id>(): boolean` in which a `Return` sets the function's `result` local and returns true, each call of it returns in turn when it returns true (`if flow<Id>() then return result end` in a function that returns a value, `return` in one that does not, `return true` inside another flow function); and a function that returns a value ends with `return nil` unless its body always returns, as Luau's `UnreachableCode` lint judges it, so every path returns one value and the text adds no unreachable line. A graph without methods, Returns or the opt-in keeps M24's text byte for byte, so `GraphImporter`'s version stays 1. Statements run in their flow's order, each with its own `do ... end` block computing the pure values it reads (`v<Id>_<Pin>`, assigned again rather than declared in a nested block that computes them anew), its outputs the function's locals `n<Id>_<Pin>`; a node entered by several exec links is a local function `flow<Id>`; every computed value is also written to `self.__GraphLive["<Id>.<Pin>"]` for the editor's live values (`ScriptEngine::ReadInstanceValues`). Typed values that reach an Any input whose Luau type is a table or a union, or `==` between two typed operands, are cast to `any`, so every graph that validates type-checks. A member a table lacks reads nil; indexing nil, a member an engine value lacks, or calling nil or a missing method is Luau's run-time error at the node's line (M39). `LineNodes` maps each line to its node, so a compile, type or runtime error at a line of the text names its node. The text is built without recursion per node; a flow nested more than 64 blocks deep is `ValidateGraph`'s issue at the statement that first passes the limit, since Luau's parser recurses once per block, and so is a text larger than 8 MiB at the statement whose code passes it, since each statement evaluates again the values it reads; a text beyond another of Luau's limits (200 locals a function) fails its compile at a line of the node that exceeds it.
- **The import** reads the document strictly, validates it against a library built from the editor's frozen pure script API (§11.2's load-time environment; an import without the editor builds one of its own), transpiles it, type-checks the text under the `.graph` path (the findings prefixed with their node) and extracts it through `LoadTimeVm::Extract`, whose VM binds the same API, which must give a Behaviour named the graph's Name; the script check is published before anything can fail, its environment hash the declarations', so every graph is imported again when the script API changes. `Import.Dependencies` are the graph's Asset literals.
- **The script source rule** (`IsScriptSourcePath`, `Asset/ScriptData.h`): a `project://Assets/` path ending in `.luau` or `.graph` is a script's origin at every site that takes one (the extraction's request, the sandbox's module rule, the require resolver's importer and `EnterModule`, hot reload's candidates and staged values, the type checker's request); the module a require resolves to stays `.luau` only, so no script requires a graph.
- **The export** scans a graph's transpiled text for `Assets.Load` exactly as it scans a `.luau` source (§14.2, ADR 0030 decisions 19 to 21), transpiling it against one library per export built from the editor's script API registry, so literal and computed loads behave as a Luau script's.
- **Live values** (W24.2, ADR 0035 decision 14): the text writes every value it computes, a pure node's and a statement's data outputs, also to the instance's table `self.__GraphLive` (`ScriptLiveValuesKey`) under the key `"<Id>.<Pin>"` (`GetGraphProbeKey`), a table the generated `OnCreate` makes first. The writes are in every configuration's bytes, so the text stays one, and they change nothing the state hash covers, since instance tables are outside it as every script's are (§5.1); they cost one table store per computed value. Between frames the editor reads an instance's own string-keyed members and that table's entries with `ScriptEngine::ReadInstanceValues(entity, slot)`, which runs no Luau and allocates nothing in the VM (raw reads only, no metamethod, no string, table or userdata pushed), so neither the heap nor the collector's debt changes and every later result of the session, its state hash included, is what it would have been without the read; values come back in reflection's JSON spelling with their type names, a table, function, proxy, non-finite number or string that is not valid UTF-8 as null, at most `MaxScriptInstanceValues` (16,384) a list. `graph.liveValues` (§13.5) serves them by node and pin, with the members and the instance's retained script errors mapped to nodes through the graph's current text, and the Graph Editor polls it once a frame while a play session runs and its graph is open, as the inspector does for a graph slot of the one selected entity, naming the slot by the graph's current behaviour name as the method matches it (§12.2; ADR 0035's milestone review), each read at the editor's next safe point between frames, so live values take no `PlaySessionPhase`. The method names a slot by its behaviour name and reads the first slot of that name, so of two graph slots of one name on an entity only the first can be read live: the inspector says so on the second, and the Graph Editor, when the slot read holds another graph than the one open, shows none of its values and says why (ADR 0035 decision 14, a kept limit).

---

## 12. Editor

### 12.1 Structure
- **`EditorCore`** (static library, no ImGui, linked by `Editor` and `Tests`): `EditorContext` (project, up to `MaxOpenScenes` (16) **open scenes** in tab order, one of them active (M20, `Docs/Decisions/0031-m20-contract.md` decision 13): each open scene is its own document, with its own scene, path, dirty and on-disk flags, `CommandHistory`, revision and `SelectionSet`, and has an `OpenSceneId` that is never reused; `GetScene()` and every member that names "the open scene" address the active scene, or a request's scene target while an `EditorSceneTargetScope` is open; a revision names one state of one open scene, never another's; opening a scene without `keepOpen` replaces the active one, which requires saving or discarding it (§13.5); `PlaySession`, which plays the active scene, diagnostics, editor camera state), `ProjectManager` (create from template, open, recent list in `user://Editor.json`), commands (§12.3), `AutomationServer` and all editor method handlers (`EditorCore/Automation/*Methods.cpp`), `Exporter`, `ScriptTypeChecker`, `ProjectValidator` (§13.7), `Autosave` (per open scene, §4.13).
- **`Editor`** (executable): `EditorApp`, `EditorLayer`, panels, gizmo, drawers. Panels read `EditorContext` every frame and never treat ImGui state as truth; every mutation goes through `EditorContext::Execute(Scope<Command>)`, the same entry point automation uses.
  M10 keeps CPU camera, gizmo-preview, reflected-edit, viewport and UI-state logic in EditorCore for tests without ImGui; the panels, ImGuizmo adapter and drawers remain in Editor (ADR 0018). A gizmo gesture changes an owned scene preview, then commits once on release; a conflicting edit cancels it before any live write. Preview state is excluded from simulation and autosave.
- CLI: `Editor [--help | -h]`, or `Editor [--project <path.eproj or its directory>] [--read-only] [--strict] [--headless] [--renderer vulkan|none] [--automation[=port]] [--automation-test-hooks] [--batch f.jsonl [--id-seed N]] [--run-tests [--filter F] [--junit out.xml]] [--check-scripts] [--upgrade] [--export <dir> --config Debug|Release|Dist [--testing] [--smoke-test] [--export-report out.json]] [--export-root <dir>] [--bake-engine-assets] [--engine-cache-dir <dir>] [--dump-reference <dir>] [--frames N [--viewport-screenshot <path>] [--editor-screenshot <path>]] [--gpu-validation] [--vulkan-api=1.3]`, plus the engine options of §13.9. `ParseEditorLaunchOptions` (`EditorCore/EditorCommandLine.h`) and `CreateEditorApp` hold the option-combination rules, which their tests pin (ADR 0008 decision 14). `--help` (or `-h`, the one single-dash option, which `ExpandEditorShortOptions` spells `--help` wherever it stands as an option) prints the usage, every engine and editor option with its one-line description (`CommandLine::FormatUsage`), to standard output and exits 0 from `RunEditor` (`Editor/EditorApp.h`) before any application or process context exists, so it writes no log file, creates no user-data directory and loads no Vulkan loader; the other arguments must still parse, so an unknown option stays a usage error (exit code 2), but no combination rule is checked (ADR 0026, friction F20). `--strict` reads every project the editor opens strictly, so unknown keys, fields and components in its `.eproj`, scenes and prefabs are errors instead of warnings, a settings patch (`project.setSettings`, the inspector) naming a member the settings do not have is refused instead of dropped with a warning, and a scene or prefab that does not load strictly for any reason refuses the project, naming the file (§6); it combines with every other option, and the feature, determinism and export suites pass it (§15.8; ADR 0025). One-shot validation is `--batch` with a `project.validate` line, and timeouts belong to the calling scripts (§4.1; ADR 0024 decision 3). `--upgrade` opens the project with its asset scan deferred, so opening writes nothing (`EditorContextSpecification::DeferAssetScan`), then runs the `cli` batch `[project.refreshAssets, project.upgrade]` with both requests transcribed: `project.refreshAssets` runs the deferred scan first, so the `.meta` files it writes are attributed to that request (id 1) and the rewrites to `project.upgrade` (id 2), each with its own transcript line, and a failure of either ends the run non-zero with its response line transcribed (§13.12; ADR 0026 decision 11). `--export` exits 0 when it exported, 1 when the export failed, 3 when the project does not open, its lock is held or a build output is missing (`Exporter::IsMissingBuildOutput`), and 2 for a usage error, `--frames` included (a frame limit would end the run before the export); an editor that shuts down while its export still runs finishes it as a failure (exit 1, the report written). It never replaces the project, the checkout, the working directory, the user-data root, a file-system root or a non-empty directory that holds no earlier export, which it recognizes only by a `Game.json` (on macOS `<Name>.app/Contents/Resources/Game.json`) that loads as a `GameManifest` (§14.2; ADR 0025). Without `--project`, the windowed editor shows the `ProjectLauncher`, and `--automation` starts in the **launcher state**: only `session.*`, `rpc.discover`, `docs.get`, `project.create` and `project.open` are available, and every other method returns `InvalidState` ("no project open").

### 12.2 Panels
The panels that show a scene (hierarchy, inspector, scene viewport, undo history, console) show the active open scene (§12.1); they read it through `EditorContext::GetScene()`, the active-scene accessor outside a request, so they need no scene parameter of their own (ADR 0031 decision 20).

| Panel | Function |
|---|---|
| Scene tabs (`EditorLayer`) | a row under the toolbar, above the scene viewport and the panels that follow the active scene: one tab per open scene in tab order, showing its name with ` *` while it has unsaved changes and the active one highlighted. A click activates a tab (`scene.activate`); its close button closes it (`scene.close`), a dirty tab first asking Save and close, Discard changes or Cancel (a scene never saved can only be discarded). The New and Open scene dialogs offer "Open in a new tab" (`keepOpen`), and choosing a scene that is already open switches to its tab. Every action is submitted as its automation method through `EditorActions` with the tab's open-scene id as the scene target (§13.4), so the tabs need no parity exemption; while a test run owns the editor they wait |
| `SceneHierarchyPanel` | tree with drag reparent/reorder, multi-select, search, active toggles, prefab instance badges; M22 (ADR 0033 decision 32): a row's context menu "Create UI child" and the background's "Create UI" list the eight `UiWidgetKind`s and submit `ui.createWidget` (below the row's entity, or at the root; a widget without a canvas above it goes below a new canvas) through `EditorActions`, edit scene only (`Editor/Ui/UiCreateMenu`) |
| `InspectorPanel` | registry-driven drawers; Add Component menu by category; the Script component's slots (each with its script, field overrides and `ExecutionOrder`; add, remove and reorder, §11.2); prefab override highlighting with per-field revert, a script slot's overrides named by their slot and script; prefab Apply offering the levels of a nested instance, outermost first and selected by default (ADR 0031 decisions 9 and 19); material and import-settings editing for the selected asset; a selected sprite sheet's texture, frames and clips, each field's gesture submitting `asset.setProperties` on release (M21, ADR 0032 decision 14); a selected tilemap's palette, cell size and chunk size the same way, with the counts of its chunks and painted cells, its cells painted only by the tile brush or `tilemap.paint` (ADR 0032 decision 26); an asset's array of more than 64 elements (a large sheet's frames, a large palette) is a clipped list (`ImGuiListClipper`) with its one selected element's fields, Add element and Remove element, so no frame draws every element (M21's milestone review); M22 (ADR 0033 decision 34, §5.4's drawer exception): UiRect's 4 x 4 anchor presets above its reflected fields (`Editor/Drawers/UiRectDrawer`: a click keeps the rectangle in place, Shift also sets the pivot, Alt also moves it to the anchors; `entity.update`, or one `edit.batch` for several entities); M24 (ADR 0035 decisions 14 and 15): a script slot holding a graph shows Open graph, which opens it in the Graph Editor; New graph..., a button beside the slot's Script picker, creates a graph in `Assets/Scripts/` and puts it in that slot of every selected entity as one `edit.batch` of `graph.create` and the slots' `entity.update` (`EditorCore/Inspector/ScriptSlotList`'s `MakeScriptSlotGraph`), one undo step, then opens it; during play, a graph slot of the one selected entity shows its fields' and variables' live values (`graph.liveValues` through `EditorCore/Graph/GraphLiveView`, §11.12), naming the slot by the graph's current behaviour name, as the method matches it, so a rename during a lockstep play keeps them, and in a simulation, which runs no behaviours, says it has none; M26 (ADR 0037 decision 20): a Terrain of one selected edit-scene entity shows "Import heightmap..." (`Editor/Tools/TerrainHeightmapImport`): the FileDialog API chooses a 16-bit PNG or a RAW, and `terrain.importHeightmap` converts it into the terrain's own heightfield (replaced in place, its handle kept) or, for a terrain without one of the project, into the first free `Assets/Terrain/<stem>.heightfield` (`-<n>` from 2, never replacing a file), which `entity.update` then assigns, a second undo step |
| `SceneViewportPanel` | `EditorCamera` (orbit Alt+LMB, pan MMB, zoom wheel, fly RMB+WASD), ImGuizmo translate/rotate/scale (W/E/R) in local/world space with snapping (Ctrl: 0.5 m, 15°, 0.1), GPU picking, outline, grid, icons, collider view, navigation mesh view (M30: the Overlays popup's "Navigation mesh", `viewport.setOptions {navMesh}`), debug-view dropdown, asset drag-drop (mesh → entity, prefab → instance, HDR → Environment, sprite sheet or texture → a sprite where the cursor's ray meets z = 0, `EditorCore/Viewport/SpriteDrop`, through `entity.create`). The 2D mode (M21, ADR 0032 decision 14; the toolbar's 2D toggle, which queues `viewport.setOptions {mode2D}`; `EditorViewportOptions::Mode2D`, UI state): an orthographic camera looking down -Z (`EditorCamera::Make2D`), pan (MMB, RMB or Alt+LMB) and wheel zoom only (`Navigate2D`), the grid in the plane z = 0 (`EditorCore/Viewport/EditorGrid2D`, debug lines the host appends instead of the renderer's ground grid), gizmos that translate in X and Y, rotate about Z and scale in X and Y; turning it off keeps the camera. A click selects the sprite its pixel shows first (`PickSprite`, through the image's camera and output mapping, among the sprites of the clicked image, picked when the GPU pick is requested; §8.10) and the GPU pick's mesh only where none shows, so a sprite wins over a mesh in front of it (Backlog §6). The tile brush (M21, ADR 0032 decision 26; `Editor/Viewport/TilemapBrush`): with one entity holding a TilemapRenderer whose Tilemap is set selected in the shown scene, the toolbar shows a palette entry picker (Off or an entry of its tilemap's palette) and an Erase toggle; armed (an entry picked or Erase on), the brush hides the gizmo and takes the image's left and right presses (Alt with the left button still navigates): a left stroke paints the entry (with Erase, erases) into every cell the cursor crosses, a right stroke erases them, the cell under the cursor found through the image's camera, the tilemap's rendered world matrix at the image's interpolation alpha (the pose the image shows, as the click selection picks tiles) and its cell size and the cells between two frames joined (`EditorCore/Viewport/TilemapPainting`), and each stroke, press to release, is one `tilemap.paint`, one undo step; a selection, tilemap or scene change cancels a stroke. The controls show only while such an entity is selected, so no editor-UI golden changes. The terrain brush (M26, ADR 0037 decision 23; `Editor/Tools/TerrainBrush`): with one edit-scene entity holding a Terrain whose Heightfield loads selected, the toolbar shows a tool picker (Off, Raise, Lower, Smooth, Flatten, Paint) and a Brush popup (radius, strength, Flatten's height, Paint's layer); armed (a tool picked), the brush hides the gizmo, draws its circle on the surface under the cursor and takes the image's left presses (Alt with the left button still orbits): a stroke collects the surface points under the cursor (`IntersectTerrainSurface`, through the image's camera and the terrain's world matrix), a new one whenever the cursor has moved a quarter of the radius, and on release is one `terrain.edit` with them, one undo step, so a stroke made in the editor writes the bytes `terrain.edit` writes; a selection, terrain or scene change or play starting cancels a stroke, and the controls likewise show only while such an entity is selected. Viewport icons (camera, lights, audio, triggers) come from the renderer (`RenderViewFlags::Icons`: `Scene/RenderAnnotations` collects them, `Renderer/EditorOverlay` draws them, the scene view's single producer); content-browser and hierarchy type icons are first-party `ImDrawList` vector glyphs (`Editor/Icons.cpp`). Both are procedural, so no icon image set or license is needed. The image is one ImGui item owning left, right and middle presses (navigation keeps running while its button is held; the first press on an unfocused view focuses it and acts); the wheel zooms the hovered view; the gizmo shows for the selection even while another panel has focus. M22 (ADR 0033 decisions 33 and 34): the Overlays popup's "UI preview" (`viewport.setOptions {uiPreview}`) shows the scene as the game frames it, through its primary camera with its UI and without the editor overlays, at the game frame (the Game view's fixed resolution, else the project's window size) letterboxed in the view, which is what `viewport.screenshot {view: "game", target: "edit"}` captures and `ui.tree` reports (`Editor/Ui/UiPreview`); meanwhile the camera's controls, the gizmo, Frame and mesh picking are off, and the UI authoring overlay (`Editor/Ui/UiAuthoringOverlay`) outlines every laid-out UI element of a Screen canvas, selects the topmost one at a click (`edit.select`) and drags the selected one's handles or body (one `entity.update` of its UiRect at the release, one undo step), leaving World canvases' elements, in their canvases' own pixels, to the inspector and `entity.update` (C22.3); no snapping, guides, alignment, rotation or scale (Backlog §6) |
| `GameViewportPanel` | primary camera at fixed or free resolution, letterboxed; receives game input once a click on its image captured it (§4.3), in view coordinates; "Agent controls time" banner in lockstep |
| `ContentBrowserPanel` | folder tree + grid (the listing is cached and rebuilt only after a change, never walked per frame), offscreen-rendered cached thumbnails, create (folder, scene, material, script, prefab, sound effect, sprite sheet, tilemap, string table, graph: `graph.create`, M24), import with its source file chosen through the FileDialog API (`Editor/FileDialog.h`: the operating system's dialog in a windowed editor on Windows, the ImGui picker headless and on Linux and macOS; the dialog only fills the path that `asset.import` takes, ADR 0029 decisions 19 and 20), rename/move (handles survive), delete to `Library/Trash/` (undoable), OS file drop import (a drop opens and focuses the panel; drops that arrive while it was hidden ask for their destination folder), import-error badges; opening a scene in place of the active one asks to save or discard its unsaved changes first; a graph (a Script asset of the Graph importer, drawn with the Graph glyph) opens in the Graph Editor at a double-click (M24, ADR 0035 decision 15) |
